newsitem.title: FRANCE: French shares could be worst hit by left win.
newsitem.headline: French shares could be worst hit by left win.

text.p: As French stocks slumped on Wednesday on fears of a Socialist win in next Sunday's legislative election, economists said the bourse appeared to be the most vulnerable market if the left came to power.

Economists ruled out chances of the Socialists abandoning France's commitment to a single currency if the party ousts the centre right in the runoff vote, and they said the country's finances would not permit expansionary economic policies.

But they said the Socialists would proceed more slowly in bringing in needed economic reforms to overhaul France's over-regulated, state-dominated economy and the party would be reluctant to remove rigidities of the labour market.
"I don't feel there would be much difference between the Socialists and (the) right on monetary union," said economist David Naude of JP Morgan.
"But in the stockmarket, fears could be more justified to the extent a Socialist win would probably mean fewer structural reforms to help business," he said.
The CAC-40 blue chip stock index plunged 3.63 percent to 2,583.17 on Wednesday amid rumours that private polls showed the Socialists well placed for Sunday's runoff vote.

The fall brought the total loss by the index since the left's upset first-round win to six and a half percent. Stockmarket investors had bought the market before the election on expectations that the centre-right would win handily.
Investors have been investing in French stocks on expectations of profit-enhancing corporate restructurings that could be made more difficult by a Socialist adminstration.
One Paris brokerage last week forecast the CAC-40 could fall 10 percent if the left won.
Bonds also slipped and the franc weakened to 3.3828, its lowest level in three months, before retracing slightly.
Economists noted the closer the Socialists come to power, the more leader Lionel Jospin has moved to the political centre.
But they said he was still a long way from embracing the market economy in the way Britain's "New Labour" has done.

Jospin has said he opposes raising taxes or public spending and has said the party's pledge to cut the work week to 35 hours from 39 without loss of pay and create 700,000 new jobs will be implemented "gradually" over parliament's five-year life.

He also has signalled a possible willingness to privatise France Telecom after previously ruling it out. The party has said it will take a "pragmatic approach" to selling state companies which do not provide a public service.

But the Socialists have pledged to repeal a law passed this year introducing private pension funds which are meant to complement the existing pensions system. That would be a setback for the stockmarket in which such funds usually invest.

Economists said the party will feel duty bound to put some of its programme into action, "Why people criticize (conservative) President Jacques Chirac is because he ran with one platform (to create jobs) and governed with an austerity programme," said Steve Englander of Smith Barney.

"The Socialists will initially feel compelled to implement some of their programme. They will come back to the centre longer term, but the question is how fast and how far back to the centre they can come," Englander said.

On the key issue of monetary union, however, economists said Jospin is unlikely to block France's entry into monetary union which the Socialists had a big hand in designing under former president Francois Mitterrand.

Jospin is sounding tough on his conditions for monetary union that involve including Italy and Spain in the first wave, a "solidarity pact on growth" and an "economic government" to counter the European central bank.
But that could be campaign rhetoric, they say.

"I think what Jospin has been saying is electoral rhetoric," said Marie Owens-Thomsen of Dresdner Kleinwort Benson. "Once Jospin has to deal with (Chancellor Helmut) Kohl face to face he will fall into line on those issues."

The worst scenario would be if the Communists, with whom the Socialists are tactically allied, played a major role in a Socialist-led administration, economists said. The Communists reject monetary union.

But Socialist Jacques Delors, former European Commission president, said recently if the Communists wanted to govern with the Socialists, "they will have to align themselves on the Socialist position".
